chapters.situation: Gandhi has called off mass civil disobedience after the April riots and is training volunteers, while martial law rages in the Punjab.
chapters.summary: Under Punjab martial law, special tribunals impose unjust sentences and people in Amritsar are made to crawl on their bellies, which Gandhi finds even worse than the Jallianwala Bagh massacre. Refused permission to enter, he decides that breaking the ban now would only fan the flames. When Horniman of the Bombay Chronicle is deported and the paper suppressed, Gandhi takes over Young India and the Gujarati Navajivan, publishes both from Ahmedabad on his own press, and refuses advertisements. Each reaches about 40,000 readers.

updates.gandhi: Stays out of the Punjab rather than inflame it. Becomes editor of Young India and Navajivan.
updates.horniman: Deported by the government, which Gandhi calls a foul act; the Chronicle is suspended.
updates.sobani: Hands control of Young India to Gandhi.
updates.shankarlal: Hands control of Young India to Gandhi.
updates.indulal: Gives Navajivan to Gandhi and works on it.
updates.punjab: Under martial law: special tribunals, unjust sentences, the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, and people forced to crawl in Amritsar.
updates.youngindia: Edited by Gandhi from 1919 and moved to Ahmedabad. No advertisements; about 40,000 copies each.
updates.indianopinion: Gandhi's experience with it taught him a paper needs its own press.
updates.hunter: Martial law in the Punjab means 'no law'.
updates.satyagraha: Gandhi uses the journals to teach the inner meaning of satyagraha.

status.gandhi: Editor of Young India and Navajivan

chapters.situation: Gandhi has been kept out of the Punjab for months while martial law atrocities are reported.
chapters.summary: O'Dwyer blames Gandhi for the troubles, and some young Punjabis threaten to kill him for suspending civil disobedience. When the Viceroy finally lets him in, all Lahore turns out to welcome him. With Malaviya, Shraddhanand and Motilal Nehru, whom he now meets closely, the Congress boycotts the government's Hunter Committee and sets up its own inquiry, which Gandhi largely organizes and whose report he writes, admitting nothing doubtful. Punjab's women bring him heaps of their yarn, showing him the province's promise for khadi.

updates.gandhi: Leads and writes the Congress's own Punjab inquiry. Threatened by young Punjabis and welcomed by huge crowds.
updates.andrews: Sends heartrending reports from the Punjab and urges Gandhi to come.
updates.malaviya: Telegraphs Gandhi to come and appoints the Congress inquiry committee.
updates.motilalnehru: Gandhi comes to know him closely in the Punjab; a member of the inquiry committee.
updates.shraddhanand: Leads in the Punjab while local leaders are in jail.
updates.cr_das: A member of the Congress Punjab inquiry.
updates.tyabji: Abbas Tyabji serves on the Congress inquiry.
updates.odwyer: Holds Gandhi responsible for the Punjab disturbances.
updates.punjab: Lahore turns out in a 'seething mass' to welcome Gandhi. Inquiries reveal tyranny in the villages.
updates.hunter: The Congress boycotts the Hunter Committee and conducts its own inquiry. No statement in its report is ever disproved.
updates.khadi: Punjabi women bring Gandhi heaps of yarn; he sees the Punjab as a great field for khadi.
updates.truth: The Punjab report contains no conscious exaggeration.

chapters.situation: The Punjab inquiry has begun. Muslims feel betrayed over the Khilafat, and Gandhi is invited to a Hindu–Muslim conference in Delhi.
chapters.summary: Gandhi insists the Khilafat and cow protection not be traded against each other: Hindus should back the Khilafat on its merits, and Muslims may give up cow slaughter only freely, as neighbours. The conference agrees, and Maulana Abdul Bari says Muslims should stop cow slaughter regardless. Gandhi opposes Hasrat Mohani's motion to boycott British goods as impractical and vengeful. Searching for a Hindi or Urdu term for a quicker remedy, he coins 'noncooperation': withdrawing cooperation from a government that betrays the people.

updates.gandhi: Coins the word 'noncooperation' in a speech in broken Hindi to a critical Muslim audience.
updates.shraddhanand: Agrees that the Khilafat and cow questions should be kept separate.
updates.hasrat: Demands a boycott of British goods and 'something quicker', which spurs Gandhi to coin 'noncooperation'.
updates.khilafat: Hindus should support the Khilafat on its merits, with no bargaining over cows.
updates.cowprotection: Must not be bartered for Khilafat support. Gandhi says Muslims should stop cow slaughter only of their own free will.
updates.noncooperation: First used here: the people's 'inalienable right' to withhold cooperation from a government that betrays them.
updates.swadeshi: The conference adopts a swadeshi vow; Gandhi rejects boycotting only British goods.
updates.shyness: Gandhi has 'cast aside all shyness' speaking Hindi to a critical audience.

chapters.situation: Gandhi has coined 'noncooperation', though he still hopes Britain will not betray India. The Congress meets at Amritsar.
chapters.summary: Punjab prisoners, including the Ali brothers, are released to great joy, and Motilal Nehru presides. Gandhi stays in Malaviya's crowded room. He favours accepting the new reforms, while C. R. Das wants to reject them, with Tilak's backing. Unwilling to oppose such revered leaders, Gandhi tries to leave the session, but is persuaded to stay and move his resolution. A compromise amendment from Jairamdas is accepted and Malaviya joyfully announces it to the cheering crowd.

updates.gandhi: Supports accepting the 1919 reforms against C. R. Das and Tilak, then helps reach a compromise.
updates.malaviya: Shares his room with Gandhi and works for a compromise, which he announces.
updates.cr_das: Insists on rejecting the reforms, but accepts the compromise.
updates.tilak: Backs Das's position, then accepts the compromise.
updates.jairamdas: Drafts the compromise amendment that averts a vote.
updates.harkishanlal: Released from jail; he insists Gandhi stay and arranges a proper vote count.
updates.alibrothers: Released, they come straight from jail to Amritsar.
updates.montagu: Gandhi still believes Montagu will not betray India.
updates.incongress: The Amritsar session of 1919. The public cannot bear to see leaders disagree.
updates.compromise: The Jairamdas amendment unites the Congress.

chapters.situation: The Amritsar Congress has ended in compromise, and Gandhi's work on the Punjab inquiry has impressed the senior leaders.
chapters.summary: Gandhi counts Amritsar as his real entry into Congress politics. He is drawn into the leaders' private meetings. He raises most of the Rs. 5 lakh Jallianwala Bagh memorial fund, but laments that the Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs whose blood was shed there are now quarrelling. Valued for his concise drafting, he writes a new Congress constitution with proxies of Tilak and Das, a unanimous result he is proud of.

updates.gandhi: Enters Congress leadership. Raises the Jallianwala Bagh fund and drafts a new Congress constitution.
updates.tilak: Names a proxy to the constitution committee.
updates.cr_das: Names a proxy to the constitution committee.
updates.malaviya: Known as 'the prince among beggars' for public causes.
updates.gokhale: His rules were the Congress's existing constitution.
updates.incongress: Gets a new constitution drafted by Gandhi to replace Gokhale's old rules.
updates.punjab: A memorial fund of about Rs. 5 lakh is raised for Jallianwala Bagh.
updates.khilafat: Gandhi grieves that the communities who shed blood together at Jallianwala Bagh are now at odds.

chapters.situation: Gandhi has entered Congress leadership. Now he goes back to the story of how khadi began.
chapters.summary: In 'Hind Swaraj' (1908) Gandhi had hailed the spinning wheel as the cure for India's poverty without ever having seen one. At Sabarmati the Ashram sets up handlooms, and Maganlal masters weaving. Members vow to wear only handwoven cloth of Indian yarn and come to know the weavers' poverty and debts. They cannot find a spinning wheel or a spinner. At a conference in 1917 Gandhi meets Gangabehn Majmundar, a fearless widow who has rejected untouchability, and she promises to search for one.

updates.gandhi: Champions the spinning wheel without ever having seen one, and searches everywhere for a spinner.
updates.maganlal: Masters handloom weaving and trains others at the Ashram.
updates.gangabehn: Promises to find a spinning wheel.
updates.hindswaraj: In 1908 it named the spinning wheel the cure for India's poverty.
updates.khadi: The Ashram starts with handlooms and Indian mill yarn, which makes members agents of the mills. Spinning is still a lost art.
updates.ashram: Members vow to wear only handwoven cloth of Indian yarn.
updates.swadeshi: Gandhi realizes that buying mill yarn only makes them agents of the mills.

chapters.situation: Gangabehn Majmundar has promised Gandhi to search Gujarat for a working spinning wheel.
chapters.summary: Gangabehn finds spinning wheels stored in lofts at Vijapur and gets the women spinning again, first with mill slivers from Umar Sobani, then with locally carded cotton. Vijapur khadi becomes known. Maganlal improves the wheel and the Ashram makes its own, though the first khadi costs 17 annas a yard. Bedridden in Bombay, Gandhi finds two spinners, and the hum of the wheel in his room helps him recover. He gives Gangabehn a month to produce a 45-inch khadi dhoti, and she does.

updates.gandhi: Finally gets the spinning wheel going, which helps his recovery, and switches to a khadi dhoti.
updates.gangabehn: Finds spinning wheels at Vijapur, revives spinning there, and weaves Gandhi's first full-width khadi dhoti within the month he gave her.
updates.sobani: Supplies mill slivers for the first spinning.
updates.maganlal: Improves the spinning wheel; the Ashram begins making wheels.
updates.revashankar: A mattress carder passing his house is hired to card cotton.
updates.khadi: Spinning revives at Vijapur. Ashram khadi costs 17 annas a yard. Gandhi wears a 45-inch khadi dhoti.
updates.dress: Gandhi moves to khadi for all his clothing.

chapters.situation: Hand-spinning has been revived at Vijapur and the Ashram, and mill-owners are criticizing the khadi movement.
chapters.summary: A mill-owner brought by Umar Sobani admits that during the Swadeshi movement over the Partition of Bengal, mills raised prices and even passed off foreign cloth as Indian. He argues the answer is more mills, not more agitation. Gandhi agrees he should not act as a mill agent and explains that his aim is different: hand-spinning to give work to India's half-starved women and add to the cloth supply. The mill-owner, puzzled, wishes him success.

updates.gandhi: Explains khadi to a sceptical mill-owner as work for half-starved women, not a promotion of mills.
updates.sobani: Arranges the meeting with a fellow mill-owner and keeps Gandhi informed of their views.
updates.khadi: Defined as production, not propaganda: giving work to the poorest and adding to India's cloth supply.
updates.swadeshi: The mill-owner admits mills cheated during the earlier Swadeshi agitation.

chapters.situation: The khadi movement is growing, the Khilafat agitation is strong, and noncooperation is being debated.
chapters.summary: Muslim scholars agree that Islam permits nonviolence as a policy, and the Khilafat conference adopts noncooperation. Gandhi carries it at the Gujarat conference with Vallabhbhai and Abbas Tyabji. At the special Calcutta Congress of September 1920 he drafts the resolution on the train, finds he left out the word 'nonviolent', and fixes it on the printed copies. Swaraj is added as a goal at the urging of Vijayaraghavachari and Motilal Nehru, and the resolution passes. Gandhi deeply mourns Tilak's recent death: 'My strongest bulwark is gone.'

updates.gandhi: Drafts and carries the noncooperation resolution at the special Calcutta Congress of 1920, with swaraj added as its aim.
updates.motilalnehru: The first to join noncooperation; he suggests including swaraj and undertakes to win over C. R. Das.
updates.cr_das: Sympathetic but doubtful the people can carry out noncooperation.
updates.lajpatrai: Presides over the special Calcutta Congress.
updates.azad: Supplies Urdu terms for nonviolent ('ba-aman') and noncooperation ('tark-i-mavalat').
updates.alibrothers: Shaukat Ali asks Gandhi to draft the resolution.
updates.tilak: Died in 1920; Gandhi calls him 'my strongest bulwark'.
updates.vallabhbhai: Helps carry noncooperation at the Gujarat conference.
updates.tyabji: Abbas Tyabji presides at the Gujarat conference and favours noncooperation.
updates.desai: Sent to correct the missing word 'nonviolent'.
updates.noncooperation: Adopted by the Khilafat conference, the Gujarat conference, and the special Calcutta Congress of September 1920.
updates.khilafat: Muslim scholars agree Islam permits nonviolence as a policy.
updates.swaraj: Added as the goal of noncooperation at Calcutta.
updates.islam: Gandhi discusses with Maulana Abdul Bari and other scholars how far a Muslim may follow nonviolence.

chapters.situation: The special Calcutta Congress adopted noncooperation, which must now be confirmed at the annual session in Nagpur.
chapters.summary: About 14,000 delegates attend. After small amendments from Lajpat Rai and C. R. Das, noncooperation passes unanimously. The new constitution passes, though Gandhi regrets the delegate limit being raised from his 1,500 to 6,000. The goal is set as swaraj within the Empire if possible and without it if necessary, by peaceful and legitimate means, over objections from Malaviya and Jinnah. Resolutions on Hindu–Muslim unity, removing untouchability, and khadi also pass.

updates.gandhi: Sees noncooperation, his constitution, and resolutions on unity, untouchability and khadi adopted at Nagpur.
updates.lajpatrai: Accepts noncooperation wholeheartedly after a minor amendment.
updates.malaviya: Argues for swaraj only within the Empire and loses.
updates.jinnah: Argues for swaraj only within the Empire and loses.
updates.swaraj: Defined as 'within the British Empire if possible and without if necessary', by peaceful means.
updates.untouchability: Congress Hindus commit to ridding Hinduism of it.
updates.khadi: Congress forges 'a living bond' with India's poorest through khadi.
updates.khilafat: Noncooperation for the Khilafat is a practical attempt at Hindu–Muslim unity.

chapters.situation: The story has reached 1921. Gandhi's life from here on is fully public and bound up with the Congress.
chapters.summary: Gandhi ends the narrative because his later life is public, inseparable from other living leaders, and still unfinished. His conclusion: there is no God other than Truth, and the only means of realizing Truth is ahimsa. To see Truth one must love the meanest creature as oneself, which is why religion leads into politics. Self-purification is hard and endless, and he admits passions still lurk in him. He must 'reduce himself to zero', since ahimsa is 'the farthest limit of humility'.

updates.gandhi: Closes the story in 1921, still striving for purity in thought, word and deed.
updates.truth: Final conclusion: 'there is no other God than Truth', reached only through ahimsa.
updates.ahimsa: 'A perfect vision of Truth can only follow a complete realization of Ahimsa.' It is 'the farthest limit of humility'.
updates.religion: 'Those who say that religion has nothing to do with politics do not know what religion means.'
updates.brahmacharya: Gandhi admits dormant passions remain in him and that conquering them is harder than conquering the world by arms.

status.gandhi: Writing at Sabarmati, 1925–29; story ends at 1921
